title: Colorful Number
directAnswer: Treat the number as its string of digits. For every contiguous run of digits, compute the product of that run. The number is colorful if and only if all of these products are distinct. Store each product in a hash set; the moment a product repeats, return "NO". With d digits there are O(d²) runs, and you build each product incrementally, so it's O(d²) time and O(d²) space. Since d is small (a number fits in ~19 digits), this is effectively constant.

remember.pattern: All contiguous-subarray products must be unique (hash set)
remember.formula:
digits = str(n)
seen = set()
for i in range(len(digits)):
    p = 1
    for j in range(i, len(digits)):
        p *= int(digits[j])
        if p in seen: return "NO"
        seen.add(p)
return "YES"
rules: Work on the **digits**, not the integer value — split the number into its decimal digits first.
Consider every CONTIGUOUS run (substring of digits), not arbitrary subsets.
Build the product of `digits[i..j]` incrementally: extend the previous product by one more digit — never recompute from scratch.
Use a hash **set** of products; a single repeat means not colorful.
Single digits count too — `1`, `1` (two 1s anywhere) collide instantly, and so do 1·x = x clashes.
whenToUse: Need every contiguous-subarray aggregate (product/sum/xor) to be unique
Uniqueness check over O(n²) sub-ranges with O(1) membership
Small input where O(n²) is comfortably fast
You can extend an aggregate by one element instead of recomputing
antiSignals: Aggregates over NON-contiguous subsets → 2ⁿ combinations, different problem
Only need the COUNT of distinct products, not a yes/no → still a set, but no early exit
Sums instead of products with huge ranges → watch overflow, prefer running sums
Need the actual colliding ranges → store product → range, not just the product
remember.takeaway: Generate every contiguous run, multiply incrementally, and drop each product into a set. The whole problem is 'are all O(d²) sub-products distinct?', answered with O(1) membership tests and an early exit on the first collision.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you enumerate contiguous sub-ranges with an incremental product (not a fresh O(d) multiply each time) and use a set for O(1) uniqueness checking with early exit.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recomputing each sub-product from scratch (an extra O(d) factor), forgetting single-digit products, or treating the number arithmetically instead of as a digit string.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note that extending digits[i..j] to digits[i..j+1] is one multiply, so the nested loops are O(d²) not O(d³), and that a hash set turns uniqueness into O(1) membership with an immediate exit on collision.

problemStatement:
Consider a number as a sequence of its decimal digits. A number is **colorful** if the product of the digits of **every contiguous subsequence (substring)** of its digit-sequence is **distinct**.

For example, `3245` has digit-runs `3, 2, 4, 5, 32, 24, 45, 324, 245, 3245` with products `3, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 20, 24, 40, 120` — all different — so it is colorful.

Given a non-negative integer `n`, return `"YES"` if it is colorful, otherwise `"NO"`.
constraints: Treat n as the string of its decimal digits
Products are of contiguous digit runs only
understanding: Spell the number out as digits. For each contiguous run of digits multiply them together; that run's product is one value to track. 'Colorful' means no two runs share a product. Because products are over contiguous runs, there are exactly d(d+1)/2 of them for d digits — and we just need them all to be distinct.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Contiguous runs or arbitrary subsets of digits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Contiguous only — substrings of the digit string. That keeps the count at O(d²) rather than 2^d.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do single digits count as runs?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Each individual digit is a length-1 run, so two equal digits anywhere immediately collide (same product).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I work with the integer or its digits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Its digits. Convert n to a string (or extract digits) first; the products are over those digit characters.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about digits 0 and 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They're allowed and are common collision sources — multiple 1s share product 1, and a 0 makes any run containing it product 0.

examples.explanation: Products of all runs: 3, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 20, 24, 40, 120 — ten distinct values, so colorful.
Runs: 3, 2, 6, 32→6, 26→12, 326→36. The single digit 6 and the run 3·2 = 6 collide, so not colorful.
Products: 1, 1 (two single digits), 1·1 = 1 — the value 1 repeats immediately.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recompute Each Run's Product
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show the enumeration, then note that re-multiplying each run from scratch adds an avoidable O(d) factor.
hints: There are O(d²) contiguous runs. For each, you need its digit product — how would you compute it most directly?
Two outer indices i ≤ j fix a run; multiply digits[i] through digits[j] in a fresh inner loop to get the product.
Collect every product. If you ever produce a value already collected, it isn't colorful. Re-multiplying each run is an extra O(d), making this O(d³).
approaches.complexityReasoning: O(d²) runs, and recomputing each product walks up to O(d) digits → O(d³) time. The set of products holds up to d(d+1)/2 values → O(d²) space.
approaches.explanation:
Enumerate every contiguous run with two indices `i ≤ j`, and for each run multiply `digits[i] · digits[i+1] · … · digits[j]` in a dedicated inner loop. Push each product into a set; if a product is already present, the number is not colorful.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** The definition is 'product of every contiguous run is distinct', so the literal translation fixes a run and computes its product directly.

**Why it's wasteful.** Computing the product of `digits[i..j]` from scratch repeats the multiplications already done for `digits[i..j-1]`. That third loop is pure redundancy — the product of the longer run is just the shorter run's product times one more digit.

**The bridge to optimal.** Carry the running product across the inner loop instead of recomputing it. That single change drops the cube to a square.
approaches.insight: The product of digits[i..j] equals the product of digits[i..j-1] times digits[j]. Recomputing from i every time throws that away — keeping a running product is the whole optimisation.

approaches.name: Incremental Product with a Hash Set (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — frame it as 'extend the running product by one digit and dedupe in a set'.
hints: Don't recompute digits[i..j] each time. As j advances, how does the product change?
Fix the start i, set product = 1, and for each j from i onward multiply product by digits[j] once.
Check the running product against the set before inserting; the first repeat means not colorful, so return immediately.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two loops over the d digits with O(1) work per (i, j) pair = O(d²) time. The set stores up to d(d+1)/2 products → O(d²) space. Since d ≤ ~10 for a 32-bit integer, this is effectively constant in practice.
approaches.explanation:
Fix a start index `i`, initialise `product = 1`, then sweep `j` from `i` to the end, multiplying `product` by `digits[j]` exactly once per step. After each multiply, the running `product` is precisely the product of run `digits[i..j]`. Check it against the set; if present, return `"NO"`; otherwise add it.

**Why the running product is the key.** Extending the run by one digit is one multiplication: `product(i..j) = product(i..j-1) · digit[j]`. Carrying `product` across the inner loop removes the third loop of the brute force, turning O(d³) into O(d²).

**Why a set with early exit.** We only need to know whether any product repeats. A hash set answers 'seen this product?' in O(1), and the moment a duplicate appears the answer is settled — no need to enumerate the rest.

**Why single digits matter.** When `j == i` the run is one digit, so each digit's own value enters the set. That's why `11` fails instantly: the second `1` reproduces product `1`, as does the run `1·1`.

**Overflow note.** Products of up to ~10 digits (each ≤ 9) stay well within a 64-bit `long`, but say it aloud — for very long digit strings you'd reach for big integers (Python handles this natively).
approaches.insight: This is the canonical 'all O(n²) contiguous aggregates distinct?' shape: enumerate ranges, carry the aggregate incrementally, and dedupe with a set. The same skeleton answers distinct subarray sums or XORs — only the combine operation changes.

pitfalls: Resetting product inside the wrong loop — it must reset for each new start index i.
Using a 32-bit int that overflows on long digit runs — use long or big integers.
Forgetting that 0 and repeated 1s are frequent, instant collision sources.

commonMistakes: Recomputing each run's product from scratch instead of carrying a running product.
Operating on the integer value rather than its decimal digits.
Overlooking single-digit runs, which catch repeated digits and zeros immediately.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recomputing the product every run
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The product of digits[i..j] is just digits[i..j-1] times one more digit. A third loop to re-multiply is pure redundancy and makes it O(d³).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Resetting the running product in the wrong place
commonMistakesDetailed.why: product must start at 1 for each new start index i. Resetting it inside the j-loop discards the running value; never resetting carries products across unrelated runs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on long digit runs
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Products of many digits can exceed 32-bit range. Use a 64-bit long (Java) or Python's arbitrary-precision ints to keep comparisons correct.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
int product = 1;
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
Set<Long> seen = new HashSet<>();
long product = 1;

patternNote: Enumerate-all-contiguous-ranges with an incremental aggregate and a dedupe set. Whenever every sub-range's sum/product/xor must be unique (or counted), fix the start, carry the aggregate as you extend the end, and use a hash set for O(1) membership. The incremental carry is what keeps it O(n²) instead of O(n³).
